pack.title: Unit 8.0 Supporting Network Management
pack.notes: WIP: written without class materials; needs a pass once they are made.

flashcards.definition: The class of diagram that documents where a site's cabling and assets are, including cable maps, port location diagrams, and rack diagrams; it needs a labeling system to make sense.
A simplified schematic, not drawn to scale, that shows how the network is organized into zones and subnets instead of where its devices and cables sit.
Records the mounted position of each appliance in the rack, labeled with key details such as service tags, port IDs, and links.
An accurate drawing of the building that shows how wires are routed through conduit from telecommunications closets to work areas, marking each run and wall port.
A physical diagram that follows each work-area wall port back to its port on the patch panel or distribution frame, and from there to its switch port.
The per-layer schematic of asset IDs, cable links, and wall, patch panel, and switch port IDs, with color or line style showing each cable type.
The per-layer schematic of how switches and routers interconnect, with asset IDs or management IPs, interface IDs, and each link's protocol and bandwidth.
The per-layer schematic of router and firewall interface IP addresses, each link's network ID and netmask, VLAN IDs, and DHCP scopes.

A record of the organization's hardware, such as appliances, servers, workstations, and cabling, and its software, such as operating systems and applications, linked to each item's warranty and support documents.

Tracking usage so every installation complies with the vendor's agreement; on a switch or router, an activation problem can limit ports, routes, or routing protocols, and trial features stop when the grace period ends.
Software that scans DHCP and DNS servers and logs which addresses are in use to a database, replacing hand-kept spreadsheets, and can often reconfigure those servers remotely.
A contract setting out the detailed terms of an ongoing service, such as its scope, performance, and each side's responsibilities, between a provider and a customer or between internal departments.

The legal basis for protecting information assets: it sets the permitted uses of sensitive data, storage and distribution limits, and penalties for breaches; employment contracts usually contain its clauses.
Overseeing assets from acquisition through deployment and use to decommissioning, with up-to-date inventory records showing which ones the vendor no longer fully supports.
The phase that begins when the manufacturer stops selling a product, in which support and the availability of spares and updates become more limited.
The status of a product its developer or vendor no longer maintains: it receives no security updates, so one still in active use is a critical vulnerability.

Keeping firmware, operating systems, and applications updated as vendors fix vulnerabilities; a host OS can take patches one at a time, but an appliance OS is updated to a particular version with a new system image.
The publicly released update package, which can carry feature changes as well as fixes, as opposed to a bugfix, the name kept for an issue caught during development and testing.
The name usually reserved for a fix to an issue caught during product development and testing.
The software built into a hardware device such as a router or firewall; updating it is called flashing the chip, and the configuration should be backed up first.
Reverting software or firmware to a previous version, such as to fix a problem a recent update caused; it is not always possible, and a configuration backup may not fit the older version.
The life-cycle phase when a server or appliance is resold, given away, or recycled; a factory reset wipes its custom settings, but leftover data must also be removed.
Erasing the data on HDDs, SSDs, and tapes before disposal or reuse while leaving them intact; on an HDD the standard method is overwriting, using the drive's firmware tools or a utility.
A documented process for implementing modifications in a planned and controlled way, with approval, to minimize configuration drift and unscheduled downtime.

Following each change through a ticket system: the ticket documents the proposed change and its approval, the stakeholders, and the change and rollback plans, and monitors progress through implementation and testing.
A systematic approach to keeping each IT system in its desired state throughout its life, built on identifying and documenting all the infrastructure and devices at a site.
The state a device is actually in on the working network; a temporary or lasting deviation from the baseline is called configuration drift.
A copy of the production configuration made at a particular time; because production may have drifted, it might not match the golden configuration.
The documented, approved state a device should be in, used as a template so audits can detect unexpected or unauthorized changes.
The message an agent sends to inform the monitor of a notable event, such as a port failure, once a value passes its set threshold; the monitor shows it as an alert.
The data store an SNMP agent keeps of variables about its device's activity, each referred to by a numeric object identifier (OID) in a tree structure.
The SNMP version that many networks still run, with no robust authentication or encryption: its community strings are sent in plaintext, where v3 uses usernames and signed messages instead.

The SNMP version with encryption and strong user-based authentication: agents hold usernames and permissions instead of community strings, and messages are signed with a hash of the user's passphrase.
A basic kind of password configured on an agent: the agent passes information only to management systems set with the same one, and there are usually two, for read-only and read-write access.
Management software that gives one place to oversee network activity: it polls agents at regular intervals for their MIB data, displays it for review, and shows traps as alerts.
Metadata about groups of packets that share the same source and destination IP addresses, ports, and protocol, collected instead of whole payloads to cut processing and bandwidth.
A technology on routers and switches that gathers only traffic flow metadata, not whole packets, and reports it to a database for analysis.
Using a sniffer to record the frames moving over the network medium and save them to a file; the sniffer can connect through a mirrored switch port or a TAP.
Measurements of resource utilization at a point in time, such as when a system is first installed, to compare responsiveness against later; system changes usually call for new ones.
Recording and highlighting behavior or usage that is not consistent with normal activity, then, for a high-priority case, announcing it with a message such as an email or text.
Making log data from different sources consistent and searchable, which goes beyond simply collecting it, and condensing repeated events into one summary event that counts them.
A server that receives the event messages many devices forward to it and keeps them in one storage location; it usually listens on UDP port 514.
A tool that integrates network and security monitoring by automatically collecting, aggregating, and analyzing log data from many sources, such as hosts, firewalls, and intrusion detection sensors.
Linking monitoring and logging products by making one product's functions available to scripts, so a SIEM can, for example, start a configuration monitor's scan and get the results directly.
A switch feature that copies frames addressed to chosen ports, or all ports, to one specially configured port for a sniffer; frames with errors are not copied, and frames may drop under heavy load.
The syslog severity code meaning the system is unusable, as in a kernel panic.
The syslog severity code one step less severe than emergency, for a fault needing immediate remediation that has already occurred.
The syslog severity code one step more severe than debug, for a normal event that is still worth reporting.
Verifying exactly what is connected to the network and what it communicates, to confirm hosts are in the right VLANs or subnets and to find rogue or unauthorized machines.
Network scans run whenever the administrator decides one is needed; since adversaries cannot time their activity around them, they may catch unauthorized activity better.
Network scans run on a regular timetable; an adversary who knows the timetable could keep malicious activity low during those windows.
The protocol analyzer function that monitors statistics instead of reading each frame: bandwidth used by each protocol or host, the most active hosts, and link utilization and reliability.
Watching a host's or appliance's metrics, such as bandwidth, utilization and throughput, CPU, memory, and storage, to tell whether it is operating normally.
Probing a host or service for a non-error response, and raising an alert or alarm if it suffers an outage or other unscheduled downtime.
Generating logs, alerts, or alarms when a device's production settings change; some tools show line-by-line differences from the baseline.
Data collected for a network adapter or a switch or router port to diagnose performance problems: utilization, per-protocol utilization, error rate, discards and drops, and retransmissions.
When the network infrastructure cannot meet the demands of peak load and starts to queue or drop packets.
The ratio between the demand for a service and its available capacity; a planning issue, which monitoring tracks in case hosts or their bandwidth needs grow.
A point of poor performance that reduces the whole network's productivity; a continual problem points to a device, and one only at certain times to user or application behavior.
The amount of information a link can transmit, in bits per second: the link's available capacity, not the throughput actually achieved over it.
The time it takes a transmission to reach the recipient, measured in milliseconds; real-time voice and video are much more sensitive to it than bursty data.
Packets that never reach their destination, expected only to a degree; in a capture, high numbers of TCP retransmissions and duplicate acknowledgments strongly indicate it.
A variation in the delay, seen as an inconsistent rate of packet delivery and measured in milliseconds; real-time voice and video suffer most from it.
A system that identifies the traffic of a specific application, such as VoIP, and prioritizes it over others, such as file transfer, instead of forwarding packets in arrival order.
Delaying certain packet types, based on their content, so other traffic gets priority and critical applications see less latency; packets wait for free bandwidth, where policing simply drops them.
A tool that works with a sniffer to break down each frame, live or from a saved file, and show its header fields and payload contents in a readable format.
A sniffer filter that limits which frames get saved at all, reducing the amount of data collected; frames it leaves out are never stored.
An analyzer filter that shows only particular frames, or sequences of frames, from a live stream or saved file, without deleting the frames it hides.
The Linux command line packet capture utility, which shows captured packets until stopped, can write them to a file, and filters them by host, port, direction, or protocol.
The open-source security scanner used for auditing and penetration testing: given a subnet or address, by default it finds which hosts are up, then port scans each one for its services.
A tool, often part of a host discovery tool, that tries to identify which TCP and UDP ports on a host are listening; analyzing the responses can also reveal software and OS versions.
The IEEE standards-based protocol that switches, routers, and access points run to identify other devices on the same local network.
The proprietary protocol that runs by default on one vendor's switches, routers, and access points, multicasting status announcements so each device keeps a cache of its neighbors' details.
An online tool for checking Internet links: a broadband checker measures how fast the downlink and uplink are, plus latency, and a website checker times how quickly a site's pages load.
A box in the cabling that copies the signal to a monitor port; a passive one passes every frame, even corrupt ones, at any load, and an active one is powered and regenerates the signal.
